title: Voltaire on His Deathbed: The French Philosopher's Last Repartee to the Priest
summary: On his deathbed in 1778 Paris, the legendary French Enlightenment philosopher Voltaire retained his razor-sharp wit to the very end when urged by a priest to renounce the Devil.
full_text:
On the evening of May 30, 1778, in an apartment overlooking the River Seine in Paris, eighty-three-year-old François-Marie Arouet—known to the world as Voltaire—lay dying.

For more than half a century, the patriarch of the European Enlightenment had waged an unrelenting war against religious fanaticism, judicial torture, and intellectual intolerance with the most formidable weapon of his age: incandescent wit.

As the philosopher drifted in and out of consciousness, an orthodox priest entered the bedroom, determined to extract a formal confession and deathbed renunciation of his skeptical works.

Leaning over the bed, the priest addressed the dying philosopher in urgent, solemn tones:
"Monsieur de Voltaire, you are standing upon the threshold of eternity! Do you renounce the Devil and all his works?"

Voltaire turned his head slowly upon the pillow, opened his keen eyes with a faint, unmistakable twinkle of irony, and whispered his famous final repartee:
"My good father, this is no time to be making new enemies!"

Even in the solemn grip of death, Voltaire’s intellectual audacity remained unconquered. He passed away as he had lived: defying dogmatic presumption with sovereign, humane humor.

moral: True intellectual freedom remains unbowed to the final breath; humor and reason transcend dogmatic intimidation.
